spike-design-system.headline: One system for a product that does everything.
spike-design-system.lead: The design system behind Spike, a media buying ecosystem: how files are organised, how a component is built once, and how one token change reaches every screen.

story.text: Context

Spike is an ecosystem for a media buying company. Tasks, analytics, budgets, automations, documents and hiring live in one product, on desktop, tablet and mobile. A product this wide can’t be held together screen by screen, so the system came first.
Problem
The product had many modules and platforms, with no agreed place for what is shared and what is local.
Without clear statuses it’s hard to tell which file is being worked on, which is ready for dev and which is live.
A component redrawn per size and state means one decision has to be repeated everywhere.
Design and front end need to call the same thing by the same name.
Define geometry once. Change appearance through variants and tokens.
Three decisions
Files: libraries are layered from desktop to platform, shared modules, local and module, so each level inherits only what it needs.
Components: a private primitive owns geometry and content; the public component adds Type, Size and State.
Tokens: meaning lives in the token, the value lives in the palette, and the same name goes from Figma to CSS.

body.text: Five libraries, each inheriting from the one above. Pick a plan, jump to any moment on the timeline, or press Space to stop.
Two setups
On PRO there are no branches, so status folders and versioned files do the job, with a changelog of what changed, when and in which version.
On ORG there is one main file. Changes live in branches, don’t affect main until merged, and libraries publish from main.
Switch between PRO and ORG to compare how one change ships.
_Button holds the geometry: padding, gap, radius, and five parts. Label is required; the slots and icons are booleans.
The public Button is a wrapper. It inherits the label, inner content and geometry, and only receives colour. It doesn’t duplicate the surface.
Try it
Switch Type, Size and State, turn parts on and off, or clear the label. The red areas are spacing, the blue outlines are content; both can be turned off in Settings.
A component never references a colour. color/button/primary/hover points at primitive/800, which holds #173F9C. In CSS the same name becomes var(--color-button-primary-hover).
Rebind one token or swap the palette and the whole screen follows, with no component touched.
Same component, different task
Table and Document share one layout: navigation, toolbar and tokens stay, only the content slot changes.

outcome.text: What it changes
Designers know where a component belongs and which file is current.
Developers get one name per decision, from the Figma variable to the CSS variable.
A new module is assembled from existing layers instead of starting from a blank file.
One system covers desktop, tablet and mobile.
Result

dropdown.headline: A dropdown that always finds room.
dropdown.lead: One component, every spot on the screen. The menu reads the space around its button and decides where to open — down or up, left- or right-aligned, or capped and scrolling. Folders open as popovers that turn back at the edge.
dropdown.role: Product Designer · interaction rules, component spec, prototype in code

story.text: Context

In B2B products the dropdown is everywhere: row actions at the bottom of a table, filters in a sidebar, a “Move to” menu three folders deep. It is usually specced as one picture — a list hanging under a button — and that picture is right only in the middle of the screen.
Problem
Row actions on the last rows of a table open below the fold. The user scrolls, the menu scrolls away with the page, and Delete is out of reach.
Menus near the right edge get cut off — the shortcuts and the ends of long names go first.
Nested menus close when the pointer moves diagonally into them: it crosses a neighbouring row on the way and the submenu switches.
Three levels deep near the edge, submenus leave the screen entirely.
Each team patches it its own way, so one product ends up with three different menus.
A dropdown is not a list. It is a list plus the rules about where it is allowed to be.
Why it’s harder than it looks

Placement depends on things a design file never shows: where the button is right now, how tall the list is with this user’s data, what is clipping it, and what the pointer is doing. I listed the cases before drawing anything:
No room below → open upward.
No room on either side → take the roomier side, cap the height, scroll inside.
Near the right edge → line up with the button’s right edge, not its left.
Wider than the room on both sides → slide back inside the screen.
A submenu at the edge → open to the other side; deeper levels keep that direction instead of zig-zagging.
A diagonal move into a submenu → don’t switch while the pointer is heading there (the safe triangle).
The list scrolls while a submenu is open → close the submenu: its row is gone.
The button moves while the menu is open → re-place every frame, but don’t flip while the current side still fits.
A long list → a search field on top. It filters by whatever is typed, but the request waits for a 1-second pause after the last keystroke — the database isn’t hit on every letter.
Long names, long lists, disabled and destructive items — and the keyboard: arrows, Home/End, typing a letter, Esc back one level, focus back to the button.
Constraint
It’s a popover, not a modal: no overlay, the page stays live, a click anywhere else closes it, and nothing shifts the layout under it.

body.text: Drag the button anywhere on the photo, then open it. Low on the screen it opens upward; near the right edge it lines up with the button’s right side.
The chevron on the button points where the menu will open — before you click. The yellow guide is the side that won, with the room it has.
Rule
Prefer down. Flip only when the list doesn’t fit. While it’s open, keep the side for as long as it still fits, so the menu never jumps under the cursor.
Folders open popovers on top of the menu, their first row level with the folder. At the right edge the chain opens to the left — and the next level keeps going left instead of bouncing back.
Move the pointer diagonally from a folder into its submenu: the dashed triangle is the area you can cross without the rows on the way taking over. It turns yellow while you’re inside it.
Keyboard
→ opens a folder, ← and Esc go back one level, Tab closes everything and focus returns to the button. Type a letter to jump to it.
Bottom-right corner, 32 folders, names longer than the menu. Neither side fits, so the list takes the roomier side and scrolls inside, with its scrollbar showing.
Long names are cut with an ellipsis and shown in full on hover; the shortcut column is never pushed out. Scroll the list while a submenu is open and the submenu closes — its row is gone.
Search
More than twelve folders and the list gets a search field, pinned on top while the list scrolls. It filters by any part of the name and highlights the match.

It doesn’t ask the server on every letter. The request goes out after a 1-second pause, and the yellow line under the field shows that second running out and starting over with each key. Typing “roll 2” is 6 keystrokes and 1 request — the counter in the field keeps score.
An empty field brings the full list back at once, with no request — it’s already here.
The same query twice sends nothing the second time.
An answer to an older query that arrives late is dropped, so results never jump back to what you typed a second ago.
Keyboard: typing a letter in the list goes into the field, ↓ goes to the results, ↑ from the first result back to the field, Esc clears the field, then closes the list.
The Settings button under the screen switches the worst cases on and off on every screen.

outcome.text: What it changes

The dropdown stops being a picture and becomes a spec with rules: one placement logic for menus, selects, row actions, context menus and date pickers. Designers stop drawing a “menu near the bottom” variant; developers stop patching it screen by screen.
Users: every action is reachable wherever the button ends up — the last table row, a sidebar, a small laptop screen.
Support and QA: “menu cut off” and “can’t reach Delete” stop coming back with every new screen.
Design system: the rules live in the component, not in each mock-up. The edge cases are tested once, in a lab like this one.
Backend: one request per search instead of one per keystroke — a list with thousands of folders stays cheap to search.
Result
[Add a real result if this ships — fewer UI bugs about clipped menus, adoption across products.]

nls.headline: NLS: one workspace for ad operations.
nls.lead: A B2B platform for performance marketing teams. I designed the main working surface: the operations table with its bulk actions, filters and colour coding, onboarding in the real interface, and dashboards that teams build for themselves.
nls.role: Product Designer · product structure, flows, UI, design system

story.text: Context

Performance teams run on a stack of separate tools: an ad manager, a tracker, partner dashboards and spreadsheets for everything between. To answer a basic question, “is this campaign working?”, someone has to join those numbers by hand.
NLS brings them into one workspace. Its users are media buyers who launch and watch dozens of campaigns a day, and team leads who need to see the whole picture across buyers, accounts and countries.
Problem
Campaign structure, delivery, spend and results live in different places, so checking one launch takes several tools.
Routine changes, like a buyer, a tag or pausing a group of ads, are made one row at a time, and a slip is easy to miss.
One table has to stay readable at every level, from an account down to a single ad.
The product only becomes useful after several connections, and a new team can give up before it gets there.
My role

I led the product design of the working surface end to end: structure and flows, the interface, and the components behind it. Every screen here is built from one set of parts, so a pattern learned in the table works the same in filters, colour coding and dashboards.
Design goal
Make the table the place where daily work happens, make changes safe to make in bulk, then let each person shape their view: what they see, how it is grouped and what their dashboard shows.

body.text: The whole ad structure lives in one tree: account, bundle, campaign, ad set, ad. Expand a level, switch delivery on or off, or select rows to act on them together.
Decisions
Parents summarize their children, so a problem is visible before opening a level. Status counters on every account show what is active, waiting or rejected.
Bulk changes wait in a draft. Buyers, tags and delivery are picked first, a red count shows what is not applied yet, and nothing changes in the table until Apply.
Launching a selection shows it as a tree, with a switch on every level. A rejected ad can't be switched on, and a “?” next to it says why and what to do.
One way to pick several values everywhere: what is chosen sits on top as chips, the rest is below. The same control works in the selection bar, the row menu and filters.
Filters move between a simple and an advanced mode without losing what was set. Saved filters and colour templates can be updated, reset or saved as new.
Colour coding marks CPA and ROAS against the team’s own thresholds, so the rows that need a decision stand out at a glance.
Metrics it was designed to move
Time to answer “is this launch working?”, from opening the product to a decision.
Tools opened per check: the goal is one table instead of several tabs.
Share of edits made in bulk, and how often a bulk change has to be undone.
Onboarding happens in the real interface. A task breaks into small steps, and a spotlight points at the one control needed next.
Decisions
Tasks lead to a result, such as a connected account or a first dashboard, not to a feature tour.
The person does the step themselves on their own data, so what they learn is what they will use the next day.
Progress is kept per task, so a person can leave and come back. Guides stay available later through the help button.
Metrics it was designed to move
Activation: the share of new teams that connect their first ad account in the first session.
Time from sign-up to the first connected account.
Drop-off at each onboarding step, to see where people stop.

Each team assembles the view it needs from widgets on a 12-column grid. Drag a widget by its grip and the others make room as it moves; pull any edge to resize it, and the page scrolls on its own when you reach the edge.
Decisions
Dashboards start from a job, not from an empty page: a weekly report, buyers by country, a budget overview, daily performance and a launch plan.
Widgets answer one question each: spend on the map, spend by platform, budget left, top creatives, what needs attention, a launch calendar.
The dashboard uses the same filter as the table, and its list has the same selection bar, tags and saved filters, so nothing has to be learned twice.
Widget actions appear on hover, deleting can be undone right away, and new widgets land at the end without moving the current layout.
Metrics it was designed to move
Share of active users with their own dashboard, and how often they come back to it in a week.
Time to build a useful dashboard, from a template compared with from scratch.
Questions to the team lead that the dashboard now answers on its own, such as spend by buyer or by country.

outcome.text: What it changes
The same model carries through the table, filters, colour coding, onboarding and dashboards, so a person learns one way of working and reuses it across the product.
Daily checks start from one table instead of several tools.
Changes to many campaigns are made in one pass and checked before they apply.
Each person can shape the view without changing it for the team’s data.
New users learn on the real interface, one action at a time.
How it is measured

Each part has its own number to watch: time to a decision and bulk-edit errors for the table, activation and time to the first connected account for onboarding, and dashboard adoption and weekly returns for dashboards.
Note
The interface here is rebuilt as a prototype on test data, so no client or financial data is shown.

nls-ai.headline: An AI that touches money has to ask first.
nls-ai.lead: A focused look at one NLS feature: an agent that explains a drop in results, proposes a change, and never moves a budget without a clear, reversible decision.
nls-ai.role: Product Designer · AI interaction, permissions, states

story.text: Context

Most AI in analytics stops at a summary. In NLS the agent can reach real actions, like pausing a flow or moving budget. That makes one wrong answer expensive, so the interface matters more than the model.
Problem
A confident answer with no visible evidence can’t be checked.
An action taken in chat is easy to approve by accident and hard to trace.
The agent must never be able to do more than the person using it.
Principle
The AI proposes, the person decides, and the product remembers.

body.text: Ask the agent, approve the change, then undo it. The whole path runs in one conversation.
The answer names its sources.
The proposal shows before and after.
Nothing changes until you approve.
Undo restores the saved state.
Switch to Read only and run the same request. The agent still explains the problem, but it can’t act.
Why
The agent inherits the rights of the person using it. A read-only user can’t reach a budget through the chat when the interface wouldn’t let them do it directly.

outcome.text: What it changes
The feature earns trust through its states rather than through a promise of accuracy. Every action can be checked before, traced during and reversed after.
Sources turn an opinion into something a buyer can verify.
The audit log marks what the AI initiated and who approved it.
Automation can grow later on the same rules: limits, an allowlist of actions and an instant stop.
Note
The prototype runs on test data.

spike-product.headline: Spike: one campaign across five connected products.
spike-product.lead: An internal ecosystem for a media buying company. Tasks, buying, automation, hiring and documents share one structure, so a launch keeps its context from the first brief to the results.
spike-product.role: Product Designer · product structure, key scenarios

story.text: Context
Spike is the company’s own operating tool. It isn’t a product sold to clients: its users are the people who run launches, approve budgets and hire the team.
Problem
Launch context was spread across trackers, documents and chats.
Results were hard to compare between accounts and periods.
Each department kept its own process, so handoffs lost information.
Approach
I followed one test campaign through the whole ecosystem to check that each handoff keeps its context.

body.text: A launch starts as one task. It holds the owner, budget, brief and links to the work in every other product.
Decisions
Linked work sits inside the task instead of in a separate report.
The brief stays beside the task, so nobody has to look for the context.
Every linked row opens the exact item in its product.
Buyers compare delivery and purchases in one table. Totals follow the current filter, so the numbers always describe what is on screen.
Decisions
Spend and purchases get the strongest emphasis in the total row.
Archived tests stay close for comparison, without mixing into live results.
Each campaign can open the task, workflow and brief behind it.
Cart recovery is built as a visible flow: focus, trigger, condition, delay and action. The logic can be read without opening each step.
Decisions
Each step type has one card pattern and one clear output.
Purchase and inactivity run as separate branches.
The canvas can be moved and zoomed without losing the structure.
Hiring uses the same workspace as the campaign it supports. A role moves through a board, and every candidate keeps their context.
Decisions
Drag on the board, or change the stage in the details panel.
Priority and source are visible before opening a card.
The role links back to its brief and test task.
Briefs and strategy read side by side. References inside the text open the live campaign, workflow or role.
Decisions
Two panes support the real task of comparing a brief with its strategy.
Section navigation stays in the tree.
A reference replaces a copied number that could go stale.
Five products create too many places to remember. One modal finds any task, campaign, workflow, person or document and opens it in context.
Decisions
Results are grouped by product, with a preview before opening.
Arrows, Enter, Tab and Esc cover the whole flow from the keyboard.
An empty result suggests a next query instead of ending the search.

outcome.text: What it changes
Different departments work in one structure, so moving between a task, a budget and a person doesn’t mean switching products.
Launch context stays attached to the work.
Any item is one search away, from any product.
New processes reuse the same layout and components.
Related
The system behind these screens is covered in the Spike design system case.

portfolio.headline: This portfolio is a product too.
portfolio.lead: A site, a local CMS and a design system, built from Figma to production with AI in the loop. The case shows the process, including where the AI was wrong.
portfolio.role: Designer and builder · product, design system, front end with Claude

story.text: Context
Static case pages can describe an interaction, but they can’t let someone try it. I wanted a portfolio where the work runs inside the case, and where adding a new case takes minutes.
Constraints
One person has to maintain it.
Everything new has to come from the existing design system.
The editor must never become a public attack surface.
How I work with AI
I set the structure, the rules and the quality bar. Claude writes much of the code. Each result is reviewed in the browser, and anything that breaks the system goes back.

body.text: Open each stage to follow one decision from a variable to the live site. The right side lists real corrections from this build.
What this proves
AI speeds up the making. Judgment still decides what is consistent, safe and worth keeping.

outcome.text: What it changes
The portfolio became a working example of how I build: a shared system, code prototypes inside cases and a publishing flow I can run alone.
Interactive prototypes live directly in case pages.
The admin runs locally and is absent from the public build.
Every new control reuses a design system component.
